umbrellas._ruled: BK 2026-10-01 09:05: a button on step 5 (Q4 · ENDURING ISSUE) pops out this mini list. Josh builds it.
umbrellas.title: THE SIX UMBRELLAS
umbrellas.intro: Every enduring issue fits under one of these six. Spot the umbrella fast. Then name the exact issue underneath it, and explain it.

items.name: POWER & ITS ABUSE
items.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.
items.issues: Abuse of Power · Imperialism · Human Rights Violations · Inequality

issue_defs.name: Abuse of Power
issue_defs.definition: when someone with authority uses it to harm people or to serve themselves.

issue_defs.name: Imperialism
issue_defs.definition: when a stronger country takes control of another land and its people.

issue_defs.name: Human Rights Violations
issue_defs.definition: when people are denied the basic rights every person should have, like life, freedom and safety.

issue_defs.name: Inequality
issue_defs.definition: when some groups get fewer rights, chances or resources than others.

items.name: CONFLICT
items.question: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

issue_defs.name: Conflict
issue_defs.definition: a struggle between groups, nations or ideas, from argument to war.

items.name: IDENTITY & NATIONALISM
items.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

issue_defs.name: Nationalism
issue_defs.definition: a people's loyalty to their own nation, and the push for that nation to rule itself.

issue_defs.name: Cultural Exchange and Diffusion
issue_defs.definition: when ideas, beliefs, goods and ways of life spread from one people to another.

items.name: WEALTH & RESOURCES
items.question: Who owns what a place produces, and who does the producing.

issue_defs.name: Economic Development
issue_defs.definition: how a place grows its wealth, and who that growth helps or leaves behind.

issue_defs.name: Scarcity
issue_defs.definition: not having enough of something people need, like food, water or land.

items.name: TECHNOLOGY & ENVIRONMENT
items.question: What new tools let people do, and what they cost the world around them.
items.issues: Scientific and Technological Change · Environmental Crisis

issue_defs.name: Scientific and Technological Change
issue_defs.definition: new knowledge and tools that change how people live and work.

issue_defs.name: Environmental Crisis
issue_defs.definition: serious harm to land, air, water or climate, often caused by people.

items.name: A CONNECTED WORLD
items.question: What happens when distant places start depending on each other.

issue_defs.name: Cooperation
issue_defs.definition: when groups or countries work together toward a shared goal.

issue_defs.name: Population and Migration
issue_defs.definition: how the number of people in a place changes, and why people move.

close: On the essay, write the exact issue, not the umbrella: “Human Rights Violations,” not “Power & Its Abuse.”
Then EXPLAIN IT: define the problem in one sentence, and show where a document shows it.

docs.src: Source: Projected: the eight states, then the world as a British atlas drew it in 1772

steps.question: Who made the 1772 map, and when? Where in the world did each of the eight states sit?
steps.line: For Map 2, read the title in the lower left and the small print along the bottom. For Map 1, name each state's continent first, then narrow it down: which part of that continent?

tip.title: NO NAME ON IT?
text: Not every source tells you who made it. When it doesn't, ask three things: When was it made? Who published it, and where did it first appear? Who was it made for? Then say what the source line tells you, and what it can't.
A map or chart has a maker too. Someone chose what to color, what to label, and what to leave blank.

steps.line: Two maps: the eight states first, then the 1772 atlas. On the first, read all eight names before anything else. On the second, read the title and the key before anything else.

steps.question: What does Map 1 show about how big each state was and how far it reached?

steps.question: Whose eyes are you looking through on the 1772 map?
steps.line: Read the small print along the bottom and the key in the lower right. Which countries get a color, and which places are left in plain black outline?

steps.question: What bigger issue does the blank part of Map 2 raise?

docs.title: Aurangzeb and religious toleration
docs.src: Source: Donald J. Johnson et al., Through Indian Eyes, Apex Press, 1999 (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography II Regents Exam, June 2026

steps.question: When was this book written, and what years is it describing?
steps.line: The source line has two years in it, and only one is when the book was written. For when it's describing, the KEY VOCABULARY on Day 2 gives Aurangzeb's years.
Eight sentences. Moghul is an older spelling of Mughal; the brackets tell you. A devout person is deeply religious. Mark each thing Aurangzeb changed as you go.

steps.question: What did Aurangzeb change, and what does the author say it did to the empire?
steps.line: Mark each thing he dismissed, banned or brought back. Then find the author's judgment in the last three sentences.

steps.question: Who gets to speak in this passage, and who doesn't?
steps.line: The source line tells you who is talking, and when. Then list everyone the passage talks about but never lets speak, and ask what words they'd use instead of "oppressive."

steps.question: What bigger issue do Aurangzeb's choices raise?
steps.line: Clue words: "oppressive measures." Open the Six Umbrellas and ask which umbrella question that phrase answers.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 2's questions in your casefile, starting on page 5. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
docs.before: Aurangzeb was the last Mughal emperor to rule the whole empire. He reversed the policy his predecessors had followed for over a century. Read what he changed.
text: Unfortunately, the last great Moghul [Mughal] ruler, Aurangzeb, opposed religious toleration. A devout Muslim and a Puritan in his habits, Aurangzeb dismissed the court musicians, artists, and historians. He discouraged poets, who “dealt in falsehood”; banned history, which “gave rise to feelings of undue pride”; and suppressed drinking and gambling. His military campaigns drained his resources. He also dismissed the Hindu clerks in his service and reimposed a poll tax on all “unbelievers.” These oppressive measures against the Hindus were perhaps the most destructive acts of his reign, for memories of Aurangzeb’s oppressive rule lingered in the minds of Hindu Indians for generations. By his death in 1707, the Moghul Empire was on the edge of ruin. The British came to fill the power vacuum.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: Sadly, the last great Moghul [Mughal] ruler, Aurangzeb, was against religious toleration (letting people practice a religion different from the ruler's). He was a devout (deeply religious) Muslim. He was also a Puritan in his habits (very strict and plain in how he lived). Aurangzeb sent away the court musicians, artists, and historians. He discouraged poets, who “dealt in falsehood” (told lies). He banned history, which “gave rise to feelings of undue pride” (made people too proud). He also suppressed (stopped) drinking and gambling. His military campaigns (wars) used up his resources (money and supplies). He also sent away the Hindu clerks who worked for him. He brought back a poll tax (a tax on each person) on all “unbelievers.” These oppressive (harsh and unfair) measures against the Hindus were perhaps the most destructive acts of his reign. Hindu Indians remembered Aurangzeb’s oppressive rule for generations. By his death in 1707, the Moghul Empire was on the edge of ruin. The British came to fill the power vacuum (the empty space where power used to be).

docs.title: The decline of the Ottoman Empire
docs.src: Source: “Ottoman Empire (1301–1922),” BBC online, 2009 (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, June 2015

steps.question: Who wrote this list, and were they watching it happen or looking back?
steps.line: The source line has a span of years in the title, then 2009. Put them side by side.

tip.title: NO NAME ON IT?
text: Not every source tells you who made it. When it doesn't, ask three things: When was it made? Who published it, and where did it first appear? Who was it made for? Then say what the source line tells you, and what it can't.

steps.line: One paragraph of three sentences, a lead-in line, then a list of seven. Waning means fading; the brackets tell you. Read the list one line at a time.

steps.question: What reasons does the passage give for the Ottoman slide, and which ones are about trade?
steps.line: Read the seven one line at a time and ask of each: is this trade going somewhere else, or trouble inside the empire?

steps.question: Whose voices are missing from this list?
steps.line: This is what historians say, long after. Picture an Ottoman merchant or a sultan in 1700 reading it. What would each one add or argue with?

steps.question: Why would trade moving away matter to any empire, not just the Ottomans?
steps.line: Clue words: "other trade routes." Open the Six Umbrellas and ask which umbrella question fits. Then think past 1750.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 3's questions in your casefile, starting on page 6. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
docs.before: A short list of the reasons historians give for the Ottoman slide. Notice how many of them are about trade rather than about war.
text: The power of the [Ottoman] Empire was waning [fading] by 1683 when the second and last attempt was made to conquer Vienna. It failed. Without the conquest of Europe and the acquisition of significant new wealth, the Empire lost momentum and went into a slow decline.
Several other factors contributed to the [Ottoman] Empire’s decline:
• Competition from trade from the Americas
• Competition from cheap products from India and the Far East
• Development of other trade routes
• Rising unemployment within the Empire
• Ottoman Empire became less centralised, and central control weakened
• Sultans being less severe in maintaining rigorous standards of integrity in the administration of the Empire
• Sultans becoming less sensitive to public opinion

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: The power of the [Ottoman] Empire was waning [fading] by 1683. That year the Ottomans made their second and last attempt to conquer Vienna. It failed. They did not conquer Europe, and they did not gain much new wealth. So the Empire lost momentum (its forward push) and went into a slow decline (a long slide in power and wealth).
Several other factors (causes) helped bring about the [Ottoman] Empire’s decline:
• Competition from trade from the Americas.
• Competition from cheap products from India and the Far East (East Asia).
• Development of other trade routes (new paths for trade).
• Rising unemployment (more people without jobs) within the Empire.
• The Ottoman Empire became less centralised (less run from one center), and central control weakened.
• Sultans (Ottoman rulers) were less strict about keeping high standards of integrity (honesty) in running the Empire.
• Sultans cared less about public opinion (what the people thought).

docs.title: Edict of 1635 Ordering the Closing of Japan
docs.src: Source: David John Lu, Sources of Japanese History, McGraw-Hill, from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2005

steps.question: What kind of document is this, who issued it, and when?
steps.line: The title tells you what it is and the year. The CONTEXT line above the text tells you who issued it.
Four rules, one per bullet. Watch who each rule is aimed at. Impounded means taken by the government; padres are priests, and the page tells you who their followers are.

steps.question: What does the edict forbid, and what does it reward?
steps.line: Each rule forbids something or rewards something. Say each one in a few words, then ask what they all have in common.

steps.question: Who is this order aimed at, and how would they see it?
steps.line: Each rule names a different group of people. Pick one group and read its rule through their eyes. What does the rule cost them?

steps.question: What bigger issue does a country raise when it shuts itself off?
steps.line: The title holds the clue: "the Closing of Japan." Open the Six Umbrellas and find the umbrella question it answers.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 4's questions in your casefile, starting on page 9. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
docs.before: A direct order from the Tokugawa government. This is a primary source — not somebody describing the decision later, but the decision itself, in its own words.

before_we_talk.title: BEFORE WE TALK
before_we_talk.text: These were real people, and what happened to them shaped the world we live in. Use their names and their words. No jokes, and no comparisons to everyday life.

text: • Japanese ships are strictly forbidden to leave for foreign countries.

• No Japanese is permitted to go abroad. If there is anyone who attempts to do so secretly, he must be executed. The ship so involved must be impounded and its owner arrested, and the matter must be reported to the higher authority.
• If any Japanese returns from overseas after residing there, he must be put to death. . . .

• Any informer revealing the whereabouts of the followers of padres (Christians) must be rewarded accordingly. If anyone reveals the whereabouts of a high ranking padre, he must be given one hundred pieces of silver. For those of lower ranks, depending on the deed, the reward must be set accordingly. . . .

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: • Japanese ships are strictly forbidden (not allowed at all) to leave for foreign countries.

• No Japanese is permitted to go abroad (to other countries). If anyone tries to do so secretly, he must be executed. The ship involved must be impounded (taken by the government). Its owner must be arrested. The matter must be reported to the higher authority.
• If any Japanese returns from overseas after living there, he must be put to death. . . .

• Any informer (a person who tells on others) who reveals the whereabouts (where someone is) of the followers of padres (Christians) must be rewarded. If anyone reveals the whereabouts of a high ranking padre (priest), he must be given one hundred pieces of silver. For people of lower ranks, the reward must be set depending on the deed (what was done). . . .

docs.title: Emperor Jahangir’s letter to King James I of England, 1617
docs.src: Source: Modified version of the Letter to James I, King of England, 1617, published on the Fordham University Indian History Sourcebook

steps.question: Who wrote this letter, to whom, and why would one ruler write to another?
steps.line: The title and the source line give you the writer, the reader and the year. The CONTEXT line says what Roe went there to get.
Two paragraphs, and each one is a single long sentence. Break them at the semicolons. Soever means ever: "what place soever" means whatever place. Dominions is in your Day 3 KEY VOCABULARY.

steps.question: What does Jahangir promise the English merchants?
steps.line: Stay in the second paragraph. Each piece between the semicolons gives the English merchants something. Find two in his exact words.

steps.question: Who is left out of this deal, and how would they see it?
steps.line: Find the other country he names in the second paragraph. Picture one of its traders in the same port reading this letter.

steps.question: How much should a ruler let foreigners in? How is Jahangir's answer different from Document 4's?
steps.line: Put this letter next to Document 4. Open the Six Umbrellas and find the umbrella question this letter answers. Then look past 1750.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 5's questions in your casefile, starting on page 10. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
docs.before: In 1614 King James I of England sent a diplomat, Sir Thomas Roe, to the Mughal emperor Jahangir to negotiate a trade treaty. It worked. This is Jahangir’s reply. Read it beside the edict you just read.
text: The letter of love and friendship which you sent and the presents, tokens of your good affections toward me, I have received by the hands of your ambassador, Sir Thomas Roe (who well deserves to be your trusted servant), delivered to me in an acceptable and happy hour; upon which mine eyes were so fixed that I could not easily remove them to any other object, and have accepted them with great joy and delight.

Upon which assurance of your royal love I have given my general command to all the kingdoms and ports of my dominions to receive all the merchants of the English nation as the subjects of my friend; that in what place soever they choose to live, they may have free liberty without any restraint; and at what port soever they shall arrive, that neither Portugal nor any other shall dare to molest their quiet; and in what city soever they shall have residence, I have commanded all my governors and captains to give them freedom answerable to their own desires; to sell, buy, and to transport into their country at their pleasure.

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: I have received the letter of love and friendship you sent, and the presents. They are tokens (signs) of your good affections (feelings) toward me. Your ambassador, Sir Thomas Roe, handed them to me. He well deserves to be your trusted servant. They came to me at a good and happy time. My eyes were so fixed on them that I could hardly look at anything else. I have accepted them with great joy and delight.

You have shown me your royal love. So I have given my general command (order) to all the kingdoms and ports of my dominions (all the lands I rule). They must receive all the merchants of the English nation as the subjects of my friend. In whatever place they choose to live, they may have free liberty without any restraint (limits). At whatever port they arrive, neither Portugal nor any other shall dare to molest their quiet (bother or attack them). In whatever city they live, I have commanded all my governors and captains to give them freedom answerable to their own desires (as much freedom as they want). They are free to sell, buy, and to transport into their country at their pleasure (whenever they like).

docs.title: The Tōkaidō — the road that governed Japan
docs.src: Source: Patricia J. Graham, “The Political and Economic Importance of the Tōkaidō,” Tōkaidō: Adventures on the Road in Old Japan, University of Kansas Spencer Museum of Art (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2012

steps.question: Who wrote this, and did she see the road in use?
steps.line: The source line names an author, a museum book, and a Regents exam. Ask: did she walk the road, or study it later?
Two paragraphs: two sentences, then six. Relays are teams that hand off, one to the next; priority means going first. Watch who gets through and who gets stopped.

steps.question: What did the road do for the government, and what did it do to everyone else?
steps.line: Stay in the second paragraph. The middle sentences are about government messengers; the last sentence is about everyone else.

steps.question: How would a private traveler describe this road?
steps.line: Find the two kinds of traveler in the last three sentences. Read the road's rules once as a messenger, then once as a private citizen.

steps.question: What bigger issue comes up when a government decides who can travel and when?
steps.line: Clue words: "barriers and checkpoints." Ask who sets them up and who has to stop at them, then open the Six Umbrellas.

docs.close: That's the walk. Now answer Document 6's questions in your casefile, starting on page 12. Use the sentence stem, or write something of equal or better value.
docs.before: The Tokugawa shogunate’s most important highway. Read it as a document about control, not about transport.
text: The Tokugawa shogunate realized the importance of maintaining contact with distant provinces within Japan. The Tōkaidō was its most important highway.

...Perhaps the most crucial use of the road was for governmental communication with the provinces. Official messengers traveled by foot, horseback (in wartime), and palanquin [a seat, usually for the wealthy, carried by other people]. The government used a system of relays for messengers, with reliefs at every seven li [3.9 km]. Government messengers had priority over any other type of traveler. They had first access to ferries at river crossings along the way, and could freely pass government road barriers at all times of the day or night. Private citizens were not allowed to travel at night; a series of barriers and checkpoints along the road kept them from doing so….

easier.label: (adapted, easier to read)
text: The Tokugawa shogunate (Japan's military government) understood that it was important to stay in contact with distant provinces (regions) within Japan. The Tōkaidō was its most important highway.

...Perhaps the most important use of the road was for the government to communicate with the provinces. Official messengers traveled by foot, by horseback (in wartime), and by palanquin [a seat, usually for the wealthy, carried by other people]. The government used a system of relays (teams that hand off, one to the next) for messengers. Fresh messengers took over every seven li [3.9 km]. Government messengers had priority over (got to go ahead of) any other type of traveler. They had first access to ferries at river crossings along the way. They could freely pass government road barriers at all times of the day or night. Private citizens were not allowed to travel at night. A series of barriers and checkpoints along the road kept them from doing so….

docs.title: The court at Versailles
docs.src: Source: The Memoirs of the Duke de Saint-Simon, ed. F. Arkwright, Brentano's, Vol. V (adapted), via the Internet Modern History Sourcebook, Fordham University

steps.question: Who wrote this, where was he, and whose reign is he describing?
steps.line: The source line names him, and the CONTEXT line says where he lived. For whose reign, read the first sentence of the document.
Three paragraphs. The dots mark places where words were cut, and the brackets explain the French words. Bestow a favour means give a favor. Watch for every place the King notices who is there.

steps.question: How did Louis XIV keep watch on his nobles, and what did court life cost them?
steps.line: Mark every place the King notices who is there. Then read the last paragraph for what the nobles had to spend.

steps.question: Saint-Simon is one of the nobles this system was built for. How might that shape what he says?
steps.line: The CONTEXT line says how he felt about it. Look in the last paragraph for where he stops saying what the King did and starts saying why.

steps.question: What bigger issue does Versailles raise, and how is it different from the Tōkaidō in Document 6?
steps.line: Clue word in the last paragraph: compelled. Ask what the King could make his nobles do, then open the Six Umbrellas and check the umbrella questions.

docs.before: The Duc de Saint-Simon was a French duke who lived at Versailles for years and kept a private record of what he saw. Read who is writing before you read what he says — he is one of the nobles the system was built to contain, and he did not enjoy it.
text: Very early in the reign of Louis XIV the Court was removed from Paris, never to return. . . . he did not consider himself safe there, and thought cabals [secret plots] would be more easily detected if the Court was in the country, where the movements and temporary absences of any of its members would be more easily noticed. . . .

Not only did he expect all persons of distinction to be in continual attendance at Court, but he was quick to notice the absence of those of inferior degree; at his lever [morning rising], his coucher [going to bed], his meals, in the gardens of Versailles, he used to cast his eyes to right and left; nothing escaped him, he saw everybody. If any one habitually living at Court absented himself he insisted on knowing the reason. . . . any one who seldom or never appeared there was certain to incur his displeasure. If asked to bestow a favour on such persons he would reply haughtily: “I do not know him.” . . .

He loved splendour, magnificence, and profusion in all things, and encouraged similar tastes in his Court. . . . Motives of policy had something to do with this; by making expensive habits the fashion, and, for people in a certain position, a necessity, he compelled his courtiers to live beyond their income, and gradually reduced them to depend on his bounty [generosity] for the means of subsistence [survival]. . . .

text: Very early in the reign of Louis XIV, the Court was moved out of Paris, never to return. . . . He did not feel safe there. He thought cabals [secret plots] would be easier to detect (find) if the Court was in the country. There, people would more easily notice when any member of the Court moved around or was away for a while. . . .

He expected all persons of distinction (important people) to be at Court all the time. He was also quick to notice when people of inferior degree (lower rank) were missing. At his lever [morning rising], his coucher [going to bed], his meals, and in the gardens of Versailles, he looked to the right and left. Nothing escaped him; he saw everybody. If anyone who usually lived at Court stayed away, he insisted on knowing the reason. . . . Anyone who seldom or never came there was certain to incur his displeasure (make him unhappy). If someone asked him to bestow a favour (give a favor) on such persons, he would reply haughtily (in a proud, cold way): “I do not know him.” . . .

He loved splendour (grand beauty), magnificence, and profusion (having lots of everything) in all things. He encouraged similar tastes in his Court. . . . Motives of policy had something to do with this; by making expensive habits the fashion, and, for people in a certain position, a necessity, he compelled his courtiers to live beyond their income, and gradually reduced them to depend on his bounty [generosity] for the means of subsistence [survival]. . . .
